outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
It's well placed for a reading group. It won the 2025 Berggruen Prize essay competition [spya-gp3g6s], and the author is a leading consciousness scientist [spya-rg493b]. My quick search found only one direct reply, [Ethics in Review's response](https://www.ethicsinreview.com/on-anil-seths-the-mythology-of-conscious-ai-part-1/). I can't tell you how widely it's been criticised or whether anything has superseded it. Seth himself says the biological view is a minority position [spya-qu7j89], which gives your group something to argue about.

Will you be leading the discussion or just taking part?

outcomes.question: What should I read before or alongside this to get the most out of it?
outcomes.text:
You don't need much beforehand. The essay explains its own terms, and the piece points to its main companions. Chalmers's "neural replacement" thought experiment is the view it argues against [spya-ahtr6e]. Seth's book "Being You" is the longer case for his life-matters argument [spya-hrydkk].

For a group, Sources › Not cited lists close papers the essay leaves out.

[cmd:mode:submode%3Asources%3Anot-cited]

Is your group more philosophy-minded or AI-minded?

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
The essay's own byline note says Seth is a neuroscience professor, directs the Centre for Consciousness Science at Sussex, and co-directs a CIFAR programme on brain, mind and consciousness [spya-rg493b]. It also says the essay won the 2025 Berggruen Prize competition [spya-gp3g6s]. That makes him a serious voice on the science of consciousness.

He isn't a neutral one, though. He defends his own minority view, which he calls biological naturalism, and admits he has no "knock-down argument" for it [spya-hj5y6s]. He also concedes that he "might be wrong" [spya-qu7j89]. Those are good passages to bring to your group.

Do you want to take a side, or lead the discussion?

outcomes.question: Does the article ever use the word "Turing"?
outcomes.text:
Yes. "Turing" appears 42 times across 22 paragraphs. It is the backbone of the essay's first argument. The key places are where Turing's definition of computation is set out [spya-cf70dt] and where Seth says "The brain is not a Turing machine made of meat" [spya-uwxe4h].

For your reading group, that section is the one to read most closely. Is your group more interested in the argument or in the ethics?

outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
It's well known, and it has drawn both criticism and a follow-up. Gwern wrote his own [“Scaling Hypothesis Revisited”](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited) two years later, and the article's opening block points to it [spya-suzdvz]. A 2024 paper, [“Is the Scaling Hypothesis Falsifiable?”](https://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/23622/), argues that the strong claim about new abilities appearing makes no precise predictions. It's a forceful synthesis and argument, not a research paper, so it suits a discussion.

Which would help your group more: the empirical case, or the polemic against critics?

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
Gwern Branwen is an independent writer and researcher, not a university or lab academic. His [own about page](https://gwern.net/me) says he's freelance and has worked with groups like MIRI, CFAR and GiveWell, and [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/profile?id=%7EGwern_Branwen1) lists him as independent.

So treat this as an informed, openly partisan essay, not a peer-reviewed paper. He says he used to doubt scaling [spya-emqjaa], and the closing attack on critics is rhetoric [spya-zyncdd]. Those are good places for your group to push back.

Should your group focus on the technical argument or on the forecasting and critics?
